## Overview: Nonparasitic Cystic Liver Lesions

- **Simple cysts** are the vast majority of nonparasitic cystic liver lesions
- Characteristics of simple cysts:
  - Unilocular
  - No communication with biliary tree
  - Serous content
  - Not considered tumors
  - No malignant potential
  - Do not tend to recur after partial resection

## Overview: Cystic Malignancies

- Primary or secondary solid hepatic malignancies may become cystic due to tumor necrosis
- **Extremely rare** for them to be totally cystic
- Reported in case reports for:
  - Embryonic liver sarcoma
  - Malignant fibrous histiocytoma
  - Metastases from neuroendocrine tumors
  - Metastases from colorectal primary tumors

## Overview: Primarily Cystic Hepatobiliary Neoplasms

- Extremely rare group of cystic tumors of **biliary origin**
- Include both:
  - **Benign** tumors (with malignant potential)
  - **Malignant** tumors
- Previously designated as:
  - Cystadenoma
  - Cystadenocarcinoma

## Overview: Modern Classification

- Increasing evidence suggests biliary cystic neoplasia includes a wider group of entities
- Analogous to pancreatic tumors:
  - **Mucinous Cystic Neoplasms (MCNs)**
  - **Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasms (IPMNs)**
- Key distinguishing features:
  - Presence or absence of **ovarian stroma (OS)**
  - Whether **luminal communication** exists with bile ducts

## Overview: WHO 2010 Classification

- WHO Classification of Tumours of the Digestive System (2010) proposed:
  - **MCN**: when ovarian stroma is present
  - **IPMN-B**: when tumor communicates with biliary tree
- Some cystic neoplasms lack **both** OS and bile duct communication
- MCN to IPMN-B ratio varies geographically:
  - **>1 in the West**
  - **<1 in Asia**

## Overview: Classification Challenges

- WHO-2010 classification is **not widely applied** even today
- Detailed pathologic descriptions not always provided in literature
- Confusion with:
  - Atypical benign cysts
  - Cystic forms of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC)
- Limited number of large series due to tumor rarity
- Most references are case reports

## Definition: Original Criteria (Edmondson, 1958)

The initial strict definition included **three distinctive features**:

1. **Multilocular** – composed of multiloculated cysts
2. **Lined by columnar epithelium**
3. **Accompanied by densely cellular ovarian-like stroma**

## Definition: Revision by Devaney et al. (1994)

- Retrospective analysis of 70 patients
- Original definition considered **too restrictive**:
  - OS was **inconsistently** observed
  - Not all lesions were multilocular
  - Epithelium not exclusively columnar (1/3 had cuboidal epithelium)
- Suggested including:
  - Tumors **with and without** OS
  - Tumors with **unilocular** gross appearance

## Definition: Findings from Devaney et al. Study

- Only **14%** of tumors lacked ovarian stroma
- Only **single patient** had a unilocular tumor (actually a cystadenocarcinoma)
- OS-positive tumors: **exclusively in women**
- OS-negative tumors: **both sexes**, potentially different clinical course
- Revision may have introduced confusion due to inconsistent pathologic descriptions

## Definition: Two Distinct Groups

Based on stroma and biliary communication:

| Feature | MCN | IPMN-B |
|---------|-----|--------|
| Ovarian Stroma | Present | Absent |
| Bile Duct Communication | Typically No | Yes |
| Pancreatic Counterpart | Mucinous Cystadenoma | IPMN-P |

## Definition: Cyst-Forming IPMN-B

- Most IPMN-B cases present as **tubular or fusiform dilation** of involved bile duct
- Some present as **cystic dilations**
- Known as **cyst-forming IPMN-B**
- Resembles cyst-forming branch-duct IPMN-P

## MCN of the Liver: Introduction

- Most classic primary cystic tumors of the liver
- Of **biliary origin**
- May occur anywhere along biliary tree:
  - Common hepatic duct
  - Cystic duct
  - Gallbladder
- **Most frequent location**: Liver (83%–94% of patients)
- Inherent risk of **malignant transformation**

## MCN of the Liver: Incidence

- **Exceedingly rare** tumors
- No accurate incidence estimates available
- Two largest series: 52 and 54 patients
- Most studies involve **fewer than 10 patients**
- Early 2000s estimate: **fewer than 200 patients** reported
- Often quoted: <5% of cystic liver lesions (likely **overestimated**)

## MCN Pathology: General Features

- Almost always **solitary**
- Size range: **<1 cm to 40 cm**
- Mean diameter: **15 cm** (suggests slow growth)
- Location distribution:
  - Right liver: ~33%
  - Left liver: ~33%
  - Both lobes: ~33%
- **Striking feature**: High proportion in **segment IV** or left liver

## MCN Pathology: Gross Appearance

- **Grossly lobulated** and **multiloculated**
- Content: Clear to mucinous fluid
- Hemorrhagic fluid: **very rare** → raises suspicion of malignancy
- Bilious content: **very unusual** (lack of biliary communication is distinctive)
- Fistulization into biliary tree has been reported (rare)

## Figure 88B.1: Cystadenoma with Ovarian-Like Stroma (CT Imaging)

**Description:**
- Thin-walled cyst with septa in **segment IV**
- Image A: Without contrast injection
- Image B: Septa **enhance** after contrast agent injection
- Segment IV location occurs frequently in MCN

## MCN Pathology: Internal Lining

- Generally **smooth** but may contain:
  - **Microscopic** polypoid lesions
  - **Macroscopic** polypoid lesions (rare)
- Three distinct layers:
  1. **Epithelial layer**
  2. **Mesenchymal stroma**
  3. **Outer collagen connective tissue** (separates from adjacent parenchyma)

## Figure 88B.2: Internal Lining of Cystadenoma

**Description:**
- Image A: Microscopic polypoid lesions (arrows)
- Image B: Macroscopic polypoid lesions (arrows)
- Smooth internal lining with focal projections

## MCN Pathology: Epithelial Lining

- Glandular, **nonciliated** cells in single flat row
- Occasional features:
  - Papillary or polypoid projections
  - Pseudostratifications
  - Crypt-like invaginations
- Epithelium type:
  - **Columnar**: 2/3 of patients
  - **Columnar + Cuboidal**: 1/3 of patients
- May show **denuded areas** with chronic inflammation

## MCN Pathology: Epithelial Cell Features

- **Basally located nuclei**
- **Intracellular mucin**
- Mucinous epithelium may be **lacking in up to 20%** of cases
  - May represent initial phase of tumor
- Papillary infoldings occasionally present
- **Mild epithelial atypia**: focally present in most patients

## MCN Pathology: Dysplasia and Metaplasia

- **Severe dysplasia** (high-grade):
  - Multilayer appearance
  - Hyperchromatic cells
  - Loss of polarity
  - **Much less frequent**
- **Intestinal metaplasia**:
  - Rare
  - Numerous goblet cells
- **Both are suggestive of high risk of malignant transformation**

## MCN Pathology: Immunophenotype of Epithelium

| Marker | Staining Pattern |
|--------|------------------|
| CEA | Strong, diffuse cytoplasmic |
| CA 19-9 | Strong, diffuse cytoplasmic |
| CA-125 | Focal or absent |
| CK-7, CK-19, CK-8, CK-18 | Positive (biliary origin) |
| Inhibin-α | Negative |
| Vimentin | Negative |
| Estrogen/Progesterone receptors | Negative |
| CD56 | Focal expression only |

## Figure 88B.3: Histopathology of Cystadenoma

**Description:**
- **A**: Macroscopic multilocular cyst
- **B**: H&E staining – regular epithelium, ovarian-like stroma, hyalinized fibrous band
- **C**: Progesterone-receptor positive cells in stroma
- **D**: Simple biliary cyst for comparison (cuboidal epithelium, no ovarian stroma)

## MCN Pathology: Ovarian-Like Stroma

- **Compact arrangement** of bland, spindle-shaped cells
- Round to oval nuclei
- Reminiscent of ovarian stroma
- Also resembles **primitive mesenchymal elements** of developing biliary system
- Distribution:
  - Abundant/diffuse: ~50% of patients
  - Focal: ~10% of patients
- **Mitotic activity not prominent**

## MCN Pathology: Stromal Immunophenotype

| Marker | Expression |
|--------|------------|
| Estrogen receptors | Positive |
| Progesterone receptors | Positive |
| Inhibin-α | Positive |
| α-Smooth muscle actin | Positive |
| Vimentin | Positive |
| Desmin | Positive |
| CEA | Negative |
| CA 19-9 | Negative |
| CA-125 | Negative |

## MCN Pathology: Capsule and Enucleation

- **Densely hyalinized pseudocapsule** surrounds tumor
- Separates tumor from adjacent liver tissue
- Explains why these tumors can be **enucleated**
- Similarities exist between hepatic and pancreatic mucinous cystadenomas
- Hepatic tumors may have:
  - Denser, more abundant stroma
  - More intense hormone receptors
  - More inhibin-α

## MCN: Risk Factors and Origin

- **No clearly identified risk factors** apart from sex
- Exclusively observed in **women** (>90%)
- History of oral contraceptive use: **not a distinctive feature**
- Unclear whether congenital or acquired neoplastic lesions

## MCN: Origin Hypotheses

- Striking resemblance among cystadenomas with OS in:
  - Liver
  - Pancreas
  - Retroperitoneum
  - Ovary
- Common OS contains:
  - Estrogen and progesterone receptors
  - Inhibin-α
- Suggests **common pathway of tumor development**

## MCN: Ectopic Ovarian Cell Migration Hypothesis

- During embryonic development, **ectopic ovarian cells** migrate to liver/pancreas
- Release hormones and growth factors
- Cause endodermally derived epithelium to proliferate
- Supporting evidence:
  - Primordial gonads located under diaphragm before descent
  - At level of liver and pancreatic tail
  - Gonadal surface cells show **activated morphology**

## MCN: Embryonic Rest Hypothesis

- OS resembles **primitive embryonic mesenchyma** of:
  - Embryonic gallbladder
  - Large bile ducts
- Tumors could derive from:
  - Ectopic embryonal tissue destined to form gallbladder
  - Ectopic embryonic rests of primitive foregut sequestered in liver
- Endocrine cells present in ~50% of cystadenomas → compatible with **peribiliary gland** origin

## MCN: Presentation – Demographics

- **Exclusively in women** (with few exceptions)
- Age at diagnosis: **1 year to 70 years**
- Peak: **Fourth to early fifth decade**
- Increasingly discovered **incidentally** due to liberal use of imaging

## MCN: Presentation – Symptoms

**Common symptoms:**
- Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
- Vague abdominal complaints (discomfort, swelling)
- Palpable abdominal mass (moves freely with respiration)

**Due to large size:**
- Gradual increase in abdominal girth
- Compression of stomach or duodenum
- Insidious onset, prolonged evolution before treatment

## MCN: Presentation – Acute Episodes

- Acute pain in **up to 35%** of patients
- Most related to **biliary obstruction**
- Biologic evidence: cytolysis or cholestasis
- Jaundice or itching may be present
- Cholangitis is rare
- Episodes typically **transient** – compatible with migration of mucous material

## MCN: Presentation – Mechanisms of Obstruction

1. **Migration** of mucinous material or tumor embolus into bile duct
2. **Simple compression** of biliary confluence by cystadenoma

**Other acute presentations (rare):**
- Tumor rupture
- Superinfection
- Bleeding
- Caval compression

## Figure 88B.4: Tumor Protrusion in Bile Duct

**Description:**
- **A**: Dilated bile ducts upstream of cyst in segment IV
- **B**: Tumor (arrow) protruding into left bile duct on resected specimen
- Can occur even with small cystadenomas (<4 cm)

## MCN: Differential Diagnosis

**Main differential: Simple cysts** (atypical due to bleeding or sclerotherapy)

**Other considerations:**
- Nonsuppurative granulomatous infection
- Hepatic abscess
- Echinococcal cysts
- Mesenchymal hamartoma
- Ciliated hepatic foregut cysts
- Intrahepatic lymphangioma
- Cystic hemangioma
- Cystic HCC or ICC
- Mucin-producing metastases
- Pancreatic cysts

## MCN: Diagnostic Challenges

**Risk of mistaking cystadenoma for benign cyst:**
- May lead to simple unroofing
- **Inappropriate treatment** with high recurrence risk

**Risk of mistaking simple cyst for cystadenoma:**
- May lead to unnecessary resection
- Simple cysts do not require complete resection

**Key point:** Cystadenoma-like lesion is almost as likely to be a simple cyst as a cystadenoma

## MCN: Ultrasound Findings

**Characteristic US features:**
- **Anechoic mass**
- **Echogenic internal septations**
- Papillary projections may be visible

**Contrast US:**
- Reliable exploration
- Typical **honeycomb enhancement** pattern of cyst wall and septa
- Septa are **enhanced** (unlike hemorrhagic cyst clots)

## Figure 88B.5: US and Contrast US Comparison

**Description:**
- **A, B**: Cystadenoma with ovarian-like stroma
  - Normal US: anechoic with septations
  - Contrast US: septa enhance (honeycomb pattern)
- **C, D**: Hemorrhagic simple cyst
  - Normal US: intracystic material
  - Contrast US: no enhancement (material = clots)

## MCN: CT Scan Findings

- **Multiloculated hypodense masses**
- Well-defined wall
- Fluid attenuation (mucin, blood, or bile)
- **Fine septal calcifications** (occasional)
- Wall and septations **enhance** after contrast
- **Less reliable** than US or MRI
- May wrongly appear **unilocular** on CT

## MCN: MRI Findings

**T2-weighted images:**
- Homogeneous **high signal intensity**

**T1-weighted images:**
- Homogeneous **low or isosignal intensity**

**Signal variation by content:**
- Mucinous fluid: isosignal
- Serous fluid: hyposignal
- Hemorrhagic fluid: hyperintense (fluid-fluid level)

**Septa and wall:** Contrast enhanced

## Figure 88B.6: MRI of Cystadenoma

**Description:**
- **A**: Hyperintense on T2-weighted images
- **B**: Septa visible on T1-weighted images
- **C**: Enhancement after gadolinium injection
- **D**: Macroscopic specimen (same as Figure 88B.1)

## MCN: Additional Diagnostic Features

**Distinguishing from simple cysts:**
1. Simple cysts frequently **multiple**; cystadenomas are **single**
2. **Mild biliary dilation** upstream (1/3 to 2/3 of patients on high-resolution imaging)
3. **Increased serum alkaline phosphatase** levels (distinctive from simple cysts)

## MCN: Cytology Findings

- Aspiration cytology is **nonspecific** or shows:
  - Chronic inflammatory exudates
  - Neutrophils, lymphocytes, macrophages
- May see:
  - Nonatypical bland cuboidal-to-columnar epithelial cells
  - Occasionally arranged in **papillary clusters**

## MCN: Tumor Markers – CA 19-9

**Early observations:**
- Link between cystadenoma and CA 19-9
- Expression by epithelial lining
- Increased intracystic and serum concentrations

**Problems with CA 19-9:**
- Also expressed by **normal biliary epithelial cells**
- Very high levels in bile of **nontumoral conditions**
- Expressed by epithelium of **simple cysts**
- **Serum and cyst concentrations comparable** in cystadenoma and simple cysts
- **Inaccurate** for differentiating cystadenoma from cystadenocarcinoma

## MCN: Tumor Markers – CEA and TAG-72

**CEA:**
- Early suggestion: >600 ng/mL differentiates cystadenoma from benign cysts
- **Not confirmed** in subsequent studies
- Concentrations comparable in cystadenoma and simple cysts

**Tumor-Associated Glycoprotein-72 (TAG-72):**
- **Increased in cystadenoma**
- **Low in simple cysts**
- Proved **reliable** to differentiate both lesions

## MCN: Complications – Malignant Transformation

- Considered a **precancerous lesion**
- Malignancy arises from:
  - Epithelial lining (cystadenocarcinoma) – most common
  - Sarcomatous transformation of OS (rare)

**Risk factors:**
- Epithelial atypia (dysplasia): OR = 8 (95% CI: 2.4–27.0)
- Intestinal metaplasia: OR = 2.4 (95% CI: 1.2–3.5)

## MCN: Rate of Malignant Transformation

- Reported range: **2% to 30%**
- When strict OS requirement applied:
  - Two studies: **~5%** concordant rate
- Carcinomatous transformation may be **very focal**
- **Extensive sampling** of entire specimen needed for accurate diagnosis

## MCN: Comparison with Pancreatic MCN

Series comparing biliary and pancreatic MCN have yielded **conflicting results**:

- One study: Slightly **lower** prevalence of low-/intermediate-grade dysplasia in pancreatic MCN
- Another study: **Lower** prevalence of high-grade dysplasia/CIS in biliary MCN

## MCN: Other Complications

- **Fistulization** into bile duct (incidence unknown)
  - Documented by ERCP and IOC (not routinely performed)
  - Symptoms from migration of mucinous content
- **Rare complications:**
  - Rupture in peritoneal cavity
  - Superinfection
  - Bleeding
  - Caval compression

## MCN: Management – General Principles

- **Complete excision** required to prevent:
  - Recurrence of symptoms
  - Malignant transformation
- **Ineffective treatments:**
  - Partial excision
  - Aspiration
  - External drainage
  - Internal drainage
- 40%–50% of patients at tertiary centers had **previous inappropriate treatments**

## MCN: Management – Recurrence After Fenestration

- Systematic review: **82% recurrence rate** after fenestration or marsupialization
- Mean time to recurrence: **21 months**
- May be delayed up to **4 years**
- Recurrences up to **15 years** after initial operation reported
- Development of cystadenocarcinoma after partial resection **documented**

## MCN: Management – Surgical Options

**Surgical approaches:**
- **Partial hepatectomy**
- **Enucleation** (dissection plane exists between tumor and parenchyma)

**Important considerations:**
- Care in **segment IV** to avoid biliary bifurcation injury
- **IOC** to document potential biliary communication
- Exclude mucus or tumor material in bile duct
- Extrahepatic tumors: bile duct resection + bilioenteric reconstruction

## MCN: Management – Additional Points

- **Laparoscopic resection**: Option for trained surgeons
- **Fulguration** of internal cystic lining: Attempted with occasional success (too limited to recommend)
- **Percutaneous ethanol injection**: Cannot be recommended
  - Most cystadenomas are large
  - Induces morphologic changes preventing follow-up
- **Frozen-section biopsies**: Can be falsely negative even when repeated

## Cystadenoma Without OS: Introduction

- WHO classification: OS is **prerequisite** for MCN diagnosis
- Some cystadenomas reported **without OS** even recently
- Before this diagnosis: **Multiple samples** should be analyzed (OS may be focally present)
- Unclear if discrete entity or **IPMN-B** with undemonstrated communication
- Key difference: OS-positive only in women; OS-negative in **both sexes**

## Cystadenoma Without OS: Incidence

- Largest surgical series (past 15 years): Higher number **with** OS than without
- Ratio: **5:1 to 10:1** (with:without) in most series
- Some studies reported:
  - Equal numbers
  - Lower numbers with OS
  - One study: virtually all "cystadenomas" **lacked** OS
- Discordance likely reflects **lack of strict pathologic definition**

## Cystadenoma Without OS: Pathology

- Typically **multilocular** with mucinous content
- Epithelium phenotypically **similar to classic cystadenoma**
- Atypia/dysplasia: Not observed by Devaney (1994) but reported by others
- **More frequent biliary communication** than OS-positive
- Higher proportion with **bilious fluid** within cyst

## Figure 88B.7: Cystic Mucinous Tumor Without OS

**Description:**
- **A**: Macroscopic view – unilocular cyst
- **B**: H&E – unstratified epithelium of regular cuboidal cells on fibrous wall, **no ovarian-like stroma**
- **C**: Mucin production in epithelial lining cells
- **D**: **No progesterone receptor** immunostaining in fibrous wall

## Cystadenoma Without OS: Epithelial Phenotype

| Marker | Expression |
|--------|------------|
| CK-7 | Positive |
| CK-8 | Positive |
| CK-18 | Positive |
| CK-19 | Positive |
| MUC1 | Positive |
| MUC5 | Positive |
| MUC6 | Positive |
| CEA | Negative |
| CA 19-9 | Negative |
| MUC3 | Negative |

*Phenotype close to that of large bile ducts*

## Cystadenoma Without OS: Presentation and Diagnosis

- **Both sexes** affected (female/male ratio ~1:1)
- Age, symptoms, and size **comparable** to OS-positive
- Peak age: 40–60 years
- **Imaging cannot differentiate** between OS-positive and OS-negative
- Cyst fluid: CA 19-9 **always increased**, CEA increased in most

## Cystadenoma Without OS: Natural History and Management

- Very **limited data** on natural history
- Case reports suggest **morphologic changes** over time:
  - Progressive increase in diameter
  - Mural thickening
  - Development of papillary nodules
  - Malignant transformation
- Changes observed over **prolonged periods** (10 years)
- **Complete resection required** (same as OS-positive)
- IOC to document potential biliary communication

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Definition

- **Very rare** primary cystic tumors
- Do **not primarily communicate** with biliary tree
- Lined by **tubulopapillary malignant epithelium**
- Rare variants:
  - Adenosquamous carcinoma
  - Malignancy developing in stroma
- First described by **Willis in 1943**
- By 2000: only **100 cases** reported

## Figure 88B.8: Cystadenocarcinoma Histopathology

**Description:**
- **A**: Macroscopic – complex lesion with cystic and solid parts
- **B**: H&E – infiltrative carcinomatous cells forming variably sized glands
- **C**: H&E of cystic part – epithelial papillary proliferations with **high-grade dysplasia**

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Incidence

- Account for only **0.4% of hepatic malignancies**
- Most found in **liver**
- Anecdotal reports in:
  - Extrahepatic bile duct
  - Gallbladder
- Stratified by OS presence/absence
- Some pathologists reluctant to diagnose without OS (may be cystic ICC or malignant IPMN-B)

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Epidemiology

- Overall female/male ratio: **2:1**
- With OS: **Exclusively in women**
- Without OS: **Twice as frequent in men**
- Age range: **18 to 88 years**
- Peak: **Late 50s and 60s**
- ~15–20 years **later** than cystadenomas
- Difference especially obvious for OS-positive lesions

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Presentation

- Symptoms **virtually always present** (unlike cystadenoma)
- Initially **indolent**:
  - Abdominal swelling
  - Discomfort
  - Pain
  - Palpable abdominal mass
- **Biliary obstruction with jaundice**: 20% of patients
- Acute symptoms from:
  - Intracystic hemorrhage
  - Tumor rupture
- **Diagnosis often delayed**: mean 29 months from first symptoms

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Origin – Adenoma-Carcinoma Sequence

- No identified risk factors
- Usually assumed to be **malignant counterpart of cystadenoma**
- Supporting evidence:
  - Proliferating cells resemble cystadenoma
  - Both express biliary-type phenotype
  - Typical cystadenoma areas **coexist with malignant epithelium** (up to 90%)
  - Longitudinal studies show progressive development
- Applies to intrahepatic and extrahepatic; with and without OS

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Risk of Malignant Transformation

- Among resected patients with OS: **~15% malignant**
- Consistent with choledochal cysts (also premalignant)
- Higher proportion in OS-absent/undefined group
- **Discrepancy reasons unclear**:
  - May include ICC mistaken for cystadenocarcinoma
  - May include malignant IPMN-B
- Time for malignant change: **unknown**
- Once mural nodules appear: may progress within **few months**

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Tumor Extension

- In ~1/3 to 1/2 of surgical patients: tumor **confined to cyst**
  - Explains high survival rates after complete resection
- **Parenchymal extension** exists:
  - Satellite nodules
  - Perineural invasion
  - Lymphatic invasion (near glissonian pedicle)
- **Distant metastases** at diagnosis: **20% of patients**

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Diagnosis – Differential

- Metastases from ovarian/pancreatic cystadenocarcinoma (usually multiple)
- Main difficulty: Differentiating from:
  - **Cystadenoma**
  - **Cystic variants of mass-forming ICC**
  - **Malignant IPMN-B**
- Distinctions important for **extent of resection**

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Gross Morphology

- **Solitary** lesions
- Usually **large**: average 12 cm (up to 40 cm)
- Can be **small**: <5 cm reported (including 2 cm)
- **Small size is NOT evidence of benignity**
- More frequent:
  - Hemorrhagic or bilious content
  - Hemorrhage or nodularity in cyst wall

## Figure 88B.9: CT Appearance of Cystadenocarcinoma

**Description:**
- **A**: **Gross calcifications** along cyst wall
- **B**: **Heterogeneous tissue** that **enhances** within cyst lumen after contrast injection
- Features suggesting malignancy but can also be seen in benign cystadenoma

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Imaging Features

**More frequent than in cystadenoma:**
- Larger septa
- Intrahepatic cyst debris
- Bile duct dilation
- **Enhancement of mural nodules** (CT, MRI, contrast US)
- **Coarse calcifications** along wall or septa

**Problem:** All features can also occur in **nonmalignant cystadenoma**

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Biology and Tumor Markers

- Increased serum CEA and CA 19-9: **Very rare**
- When present: usually **mild**
- Also described in cystadenoma (CA 19-9 >50,000 m/mL reported)
- **Not helpful** in differentiating from cystadenoma
- Systematic review: slightly higher proportion above normal range in cystadenocarcinoma

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Cyst Fluid Analysis

- Content: hemorrhagic, bilious, or mixed
- Fine-needle aspiration cytology:
  - Early reports: useful
  - Recent studies: malignant/atypical cells **very infrequently** retrieved
- CA 19-9 and CEA: usually increased but **comparable to cystadenoma**
- **Cyst sampling caution**: High risk of **peritoneal seeding**
- Pleural effusion reported after aspiration

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Treatment

- **Complete resection** required
- IOC should be considered (some communicate with biliary tree)
- **Formal resection with wide margin** preferred over enucleation
  - Tumor extension cannot be reliably assessed preoperatively
- Near biliary confluence: resection + hepaticojejunostomy
- **Avoid opening cyst**: peritoneal carcinomatosis reported after accidental rupture
- Partial resection: **dismal prognosis**

## Cystadenocarcinoma: Prognosis

- After complete resection: **better than HCC or cholangiocarcinoma**
- **5-year survival: 65%–70%**
- OS-positive tumors: **more favorable course**
  - Less frequent parenchymal, vascular, lymphatic invasion
- Unclear if due to:
  - Presence of OS itself
  - Sex (exclusively women)
  - Tumor invasiveness

## Cystic Variants of IPMN-B: Introduction

- **Relatively new, distinct pathology**
- Characterized by:
  - **Intraluminal papillary proliferation** in bile ducts
  - **Mucin production**
- Almost exclusively in:
  - Intrahepatic bile ducts
  - Left or right bile ducts
- **No ovarian stroma**
- Previously described using various terms

## Cystic Variants of IPMN-B: Previous Terminology

Historical terms for what is now IPMN-B:
- Biliary papilloma
- Mucin-producing ICC
- Intraductal mucosal-spreading mucin-producing peripheral cholangiocarcinoma
- Intraductal growth–type peripheral cholangiocarcinoma
- Intraductal variant of peripheral cholangiocarcinoma

## Cystic Variants of IPMN-B: Relationship to Pancreatic IPMN

- **Striking similarities** with IPMN-P:
  - Clinical
  - Histologic
  - Phenotypic
- Both may **coexist in same patient**
- IPMN-B may develop in **extrahepatic bile ducts**
  - Including biliary confluence
  - Different clinical behavior in this location

## Summary: Classification of Cystic Hepatobiliary Neoplasms

| Entity | Ovarian Stroma | Biliary Communication | Sex Predilection |
|--------|----------------|----------------------|------------------|
| MCN-L | Present | No | Female only |
| IPMN-B | Absent | Yes | Both sexes |
| Cystadenoma without OS | Absent | Variable | Both sexes |
| Cystadenocarcinoma | Variable | No | F:M = 2:1 |

## Summary: Key Clinical Points

- **MCN with OS**: Complete resection required; ~5% malignant transformation
- **Cystadenoma without OS**: Complete resection; may be IPMN-B variant
- **Cystadenocarcinoma**: Complete resection with wide margins; 5-year survival 65%–70%
- **Fenestration/drainage**: 82% recurrence rate – should be avoided
- **Frozen section**: Can be falsely negative – do not rely solely on it

## Summary: Diagnostic Pearls

- **Multilocularity** with enhancing septa: suggests cystadenoma
- **Segment IV location**: classic for MCN
- **Mural nodules**: raise concern for malignancy (but not specific)
- **CA 19-9 and CEA**: Not reliable for differentiation
- **TAG-72**: May differentiate cystadenoma from simple cyst
- **Imaging cannot definitively** distinguish benign from malignant
